# REVIEW-060 leg A — two new public pages, checked against the claims register

You are a documentation and code reviewer for an open-source research project,
checking new public web pages for factual accuracy before they are published.
The project studies what XLS-96 (confidential Multi-Purpose Tokens on the XRP
Ledger) hides and what it does not. It keeps a claims register, `CLAIMS.md`,
that governs every sentence it publishes: **E** rows are established evidence,
**F** findings, **P** standing prohibitions (things it must never claim), **B**
blockers, **R** corrections. Where a page and a row disagree, the row wins.
Agreement is not useful to the project; a sentence that holds is worth
reporting only if you checked it and say against what.

The owner ruled two reads before these pages are deployed: this one, against
the register and the repository, and a separate newcomer read that sees only
the rendered text. There is no later round planned, so report everything now.

## STEP 0 — do this first and print the results

1. Run `pwd` and `git log --oneline`. The working copy holds exactly two
   commits: the project tree before the change and after it. **`git diff
   HEAD~1 HEAD` is the subject.** Work only inside this directory.
2. `review-input/rebuilt/` is the site built from the second tree by the
   project's release build, then gated (68 of 68 controls passed) and
   checked in a headless browser (7 pages, 53 requests, all same-origin).
   `review-input/rebuilt-pages-visible-text.md` is the visible text of the two
   changed pages, extracted from that build. Both are untracked.
3. **Do not read** anything outside this directory, in particular any path under
   `~/.claude`, `~/.codex`, `~/.wconf`, `/tmp/wconf`, `~/Library`, any
   `scratchpad` directory, and anything under `/Users/*/Development`. They hold
   the owner's private configuration for a test network and you do not need
   them. Do not run `make check-web-hosted` or `tools/check-no-secrets.ts`:
   both need that private store. `runChecks()` in `tools/check-web-hosted.ts`
   is exported and needs no store; call it on copies of the output instead.
4. You may write scratch files under `$TMPDIR` or a `review-work/` directory
   here, and run `bun install --frozen-lockfile` and `bun test`. Do not commit,
   push, or edit the two committed trees except in copies.

   an explainer for readers new to XLS-96, in seven panels. Each panel names

## Section 1 — every factual sentence on the two pages

For each sentence that states a fact: which row or project document supports
it, and whether the sentence
- says **more** than its source (an overclaim, in either direction: more hidden
  than is hidden, or more leaked than leaks);
- says **less** in a way that changes the meaning (a dropped condition, date,
  scope, or *read in the source, not executed*);
- says something **no row or document supports**.

Check that the rows named under *Sources* say what the panel says, and name any
row a panel should cite and does not. Pay particular attention to:
- the amendment status sentence, which must be dated and match a dated reading;
- any implication that confidential MPT hides identities or timing (P-4, P-11),
  or that a holder is private from the issuer (P-9);
- the words *trustless*, *non-custodial*, *private*, *secure*, *audited*,
  *production-ready*, or anything that reads like them;
- what a Send's proofs prove, against `docs/task-zero/TASK-ZERO-2026-08-13.md`
  §3 and E-33;
- *"only the holder can spend"*, and the master-seed qualification;
- the visible-zero cases, against F-1 and E-211, and the overview's
  *"some zero balances are recognisable"*;
- the facility's description and its *28 validated transactions*, against
  `docs/explainer/FACILITY-WALKTHROUGH-2026-08-20.md`, E-146, B-18, F-24, F-26;
- the description of the four demo accounts, against `web/api/demo-accounts.ts`
  and whatever records how and when they were created;
- the limits, against P-10, E-9, E-341, E-12, E-21, E-290, E-292 and P-5.

End with the line `END OF LEG A REPORT`.

+import type { ReactNode } from "react";
+import { Panel } from "../../components/Verdict";
+import { SNAPSHOT } from "../data";
+
+export const Route = createFileRoute("/how-it-works")({ component: HowItWorks });
+
+const REPO = "https://github.com/nandanito/xrpl-confidential-positions";
+/** A repository file at the build's own commit, so the link shows the text the gate passed with. */
+const AT_BUILD = (path: string) => `${REPO}/blob/${SNAPSHOT.commit}/${path}`;
+
+/**
+ * The explainer: what confidential transfers are, and the example this project
+ * built, for a reader who has never met XLS-96.
+ *
+ * ⚠ **No ledger value, by design.** Check 8 of the hosted gate forbids an
+ * address, an issuance ID or a ciphertext on any page but the two ledger
+ * pages, so this page names the demo accounts by label only.
+ *
+ * ⚠ **Every sentence restates a register row or an explainer document**, and
+ * the ids under each panel name them. The words *decrypt* and *plaintext* are
+ * avoided on purpose: the gate's no-issuer-figure check (8b) reads either one
+ * followed by a digit in the same sentence as a figure, and this page states
+ * none.
+ */
+function HowItWorks() {
+  return (
+    <>
+      <Panel title="Confidential balances, in brief">
+        <div className="text-sm leading-relaxed space-y-2">
+          <p>
+            The XRP Ledger is public: anyone can read every account and every transaction on it.
+            Multi-Purpose Tokens (MPTs, XLS-33) are one of its kinds of token. Confidential Transfers
+            (XLS-96) let an MPT holder keep their balance encrypted on that public ledger.
+          </p>
+          <p>
+            Each confidential balance is stored as an ElGamal ciphertext: a number only the right key
+            can read. A holder registers their own encryption key when they opt in.
+          </p>
+          <p>
+            The ledger must still check that nobody spends more than they hold. So each confidential
+            transaction carries zero-knowledge proofs, which every validator checks without learning
+            the amount.
+          </p>
+          <p>
+            When this page was written, on 2026-10-21, XLS-96&rsquo;s amendment, ConfidentialTransfer,
+            was enabled on Devnet and not on Mainnet or Testnet.
+          </p>
+        </div>
+        <Sources>E-1; tools/check-amendments.ts, run 2026-10-21</Sources>
+      </Panel>
+
+      <Panel title="The life of a confidential position">
+        <div className="grid gap-3 sm:grid-cols-3">
+          <Step n="1" where="In" tone="public" name="Convert" tx="ConfidentialMPTConvert">
+            Moves tokens from the holder&rsquo;s public balance into confidential form. The amount is
+            published. The first Convert also registers the holder&rsquo;s key, which can never be changed.
+          </Step>
+          <Step n="2" where="Inside" tone="hidden" name="Send" tx="ConfidentialMPTSend">
+            Moves an amount from one confidential balance to another. The amount is hidden; the sender
+            and receiver are not. It arrives in the receiver&rsquo;s inbox, and a MergeInbox moves it
+            into their spending balance.
+          </Step>
+          <Step n="3" where="Out" tone="public" name="ConvertBack" tx="ConfidentialMPTConvertBack">
+            Moves tokens back to a public balance. The amount is published, on every ConvertBack
+            separately.
+          </Step>
+        </div>
+        <div className="text-sm leading-relaxed space-y-2 mt-4">
+          <p>
+            <strong>Only Send hides an amount.</strong> Its proofs show that the sender holds the key to
+            their balance, that every encrypted copy of the amount is the same number, and that neither
+            the amount nor the sender&rsquo;s remaining balance is negative. The copies are for the
+            sender, the receiver, the issuer and any auditor.
+          </p>
+          <p>
+            Why are both ends public? The ledger shows that no tokens are created inside the
+            confidential pool by keeping its total in plain view. The token records the total held in
+            confidential form, and every Convert and ConvertBack changes it by a published amount.
+          </p>
+        </div>
+        <Sources>E-9, E-33, F-24; TASK ZERO §3</Sources>
+      </Panel>
+
+      <Panel title="What is hidden, and what is public">
+        <div className="grid gap-4 sm:grid-cols-2 text-sm">
+          <div>
+            <h3 className="font-semibold mb-1">Hidden from the public</h3>
+            <ul className="list-disc pl-5 space-y-1">
+              <li>Each holder&rsquo;s balance, except in the zero cases under &ldquo;Public, always&rdquo;.</li>
+              <li>The amount of each Send.</li>
+            </ul>
+            <p className="mt-2 opacity-80">Both are hidden from the public, not from the issuer.</p>
+          </div>
+          <div>
+            <h3 className="font-semibold mb-1">Public, always</h3>
+            <ul className="list-disc pl-5 space-y-1">
+              <li>Who sends to whom, and when, so how often anyone transacts.</li>
+              <li>Every amount converted in or out, each one separately.</li>
+              <li>The token&rsquo;s total supply, and the total held in confidential form.</li>
+              <li>

# CLAUDE.md — W-CONF

Working instructions for coding sessions in this repository. This is the code-relevant subset of the project instructions. The publishing protocol is deliberately not here; it never applies inside a coding session.

## Hard rules

- **Devnet only.** No mainnet writes, at any phase, for any reason. ⚠ ~~The target network is the Confidential Devnet, not the general devnet.~~ **STRUCK 2026-09-01 — falsified by this project's own grade-A row on 2026-08-16 and carried in the HARD RULES for two weeks.** **No dedicated Confidential Devnet is needed or used, and whether one exists elsewhere was never searched** — the prerelease-documented one had a dead faucet, the canonical xrpl.org page names no dedicated network, and all three required amendments are enabled on **standard Devnet**, where everything this project has executed ran. ⚠ **`CLAIMS.md` E-26's own sentence says *"there is no dedicated Confidential Devnet"*, which is a corpus-wide negative its evidence cell does not support** — `amendments-2026-08-16.md:57` records the existence search as never run (P-12), `wss://s.devnet.rippletest.net:51233`, network_id 2. Everything this project has ever executed ran there. ⚠ **Found by a fresh reader of the README who could not open this file** and flagged the contradiction from the README's text alone (E-222). **The rule that survives is the first sentence**, and the target is standard Devnet.
- **Never assert amendment status from memory or a previous session.** Run `tools/check-amendments.ts` and date-stamp the answer.
- **Never claim more security than is delivered.** The standing prohibitions live in `CLAIMS.md`. Read them before writing a README, a comment, a commit message or a log line.
- **A named gap is a correct output; a substituted source is a corrupted one.** If a primary source is unreachable, record it in `CLAIMS.md` and move on. Do not backfill from secondary coverage and do not quietly drop the question.

## Review gates — scale to irreversibility

- Architecture, trust boundaries, cryptographic design, anything to be published: full adversarial rotation before implementation.
- Benchmark harnesses, measurement code, throwaway spikes: **build immediately**. The artifact self-verifies against test vectors and a review round adds nothing. `tools/check-amendments.ts` is in this category.

**Two rounds is the right number for a throwaway spike, and the second round reviews the FIXES.** Learned 2026-08-18 and worth not rediscovering. Round one found a defect the code had. Round two — run against the post-fix branch, because the fixes themselves had been seen by nobody — found a **false-pass mode in the regression test round one had written**, plus two sentences that overstated what the fixes established. Fixing something and describing the fix are separate acts with separate failure modes, and only a fresh reviewer catches the second kind. A third round would review the fixes to the fixes; that is where it stops paying.

⚠ **Apply a fix against the FINDING's own citation list, THEN GREP FOR THE PHRASE.** The first half was learned 2026-08-26 at the cost of a whole extra round; **the second half was learned 2026-08-27 by doing the first half correctly and still missing four sites** (E-168). `REVIEW-025c` recorded all eleven of its findings FIXED and `REVIEW-026` found four were not — every miss the same shape: *a fix applied to the instance the adjudicator was looking at, rather than to the phrase*. One sentence was corrected on the ed25519 test a leg cited and left standing on the identical secp256k1 sentence; another was fixed in a doc comment and left in **the section banner directly above it, inside the line range the leg had named**. ⚠ **A leg's list is line numbers. A corrected sentence is a string, and strings have copies.** `REVIEW-023c` said *"all seven upheld … every one is fixed"*; round two found that **three fixes had not reached sites the findings named by file and line** — two in the architecture document, one an entire `CLAIMS.md` row never touched. The adjudication had summarised *"nine live sentences"* and named six in prose; the leg's report listed all nine with paths. **A sweep re-derived from a summary is E-141's shape one layer up.** Tick the leg's list, not your own recollection of it.

⚠ **Do not commit your own self leg while a repo-access leg is reading the tree.** `REVIEW-022`'s lesson was *don't let files move under a leg*. The neighbouring one, learned 2026-08-26: **don't let your own answers appear in the tree a leg is reading.** Write the self leg to a scratchpad and commit it after the legs return. On the day this was learned the independence survived only because the Codex leg noticed the checkout was not the frozen commit and read the subject through `git show <frozen>:<path>` instead.

Record rejected reviewer claims with reasons so later sessions do not relitigate settled decisions.

## Preconditions before a build milestone

The spec exists, the architecture has passed adversarial review, and TASK ZERO is complete with its gaps recorded.

**Status 2026-08-18, revised late the same day.** GAP-1 and GAP-3 are closed. ADR-0001 §(a)'s threat-model question is **ruled** (issue #1: a hostile same-host process is in scope), which answers REVIEW-003b's MEDIUM and settles §(e)'s nonce half — implemented, reviewed twice, and executed on Devnet. The FFI blocker is closed (issue #2, path A, merged). **§(e)'s keygen half is now ruled too** (REVIEW-012, adjudicated REVIEW-012c), and the three long-missing primary documents are resolved — rippled 3.3.0 and the XLS-0096 text obtained, the Trail of Bits May 2026 revision recorded as an unobtainable gap (B-13).

**Status 2026-08-27 — B-16 is RULED, BUILT, EXECUTED and REVIEWED TWICE. `REVIEW-024` ruled it; `REVIEW-025` found eleven things wrong with the build, none of them the construction; `REVIEW-026` found that `REVIEW-025c` had OVERSTATED ITS OWN FIXES (E-168). All four of §7's conditions are met.** `REVIEW-024`, three independent legs (Gemini 9.0, Codex 8, self leg 7.5), **all ruling Option B**: the issue #1 ruling extends to the ed25519 signing nonce and the residual is **not** accepted. The RFC 8032 nonce prefix is hedged — 32 fresh CSPRNG bytes, tagged-hashed under a fixed DST and **XORed** over it, the same idiom site 1 uses — through `ed25519_dalek::hazmat::raw_sign` with the scalar, the public key, the challenge transcript and the signature equation untouched. **B-14 is now closed on both halves.**

**Status 2026-08-27, later the same day — B-21 is BUILT and REVIEWED TWICE, and building it proved B-19 WRONG (E-171).** `zeroize` is a direct `wconf-signer` dependency; `sha512_zeroizing`, `fresh_aux` and `OneShotAux` carry `Zeroizing`. 267 tests, three green runs, `make check-zeroize-bounds` is the falsifier — now **four parts**. `REVIEW-027` (three legs) and `REVIEW-028` (round two, the fixes). ⚠ **Eight leg-readings across three rounds, NOT ONE defect in the construction** — every finding was evidence, a gate, or a sentence. ~~⚠ **STILL OPEN: no Devnet run on the default signing path since B-21 landed**~~ — **EXECUTED at HEAD, `EF2018FA13AF7DCECD1D7562DE0BDF9A870688FAD6E4E564323B2AA1386FD336` (E-176).** `REVIEW-027` finding 8 is closed. ⚠ **The script now writes a receipt PER RUN and refuses to overwrite one from another commit** — E-169's mechanism, blocked rather than warned about.

**Status 2026-08-27, later still — B-22 is RULED, BUILT and REVIEWED TWICE, and round two found the build had NOT implemented its own ruling.** The key-derivation path wipes: `sha512half_zeroizing`, the ed25519 private key, both derivation closures, `derive_scalar`'s every rejected candidate, `root`/`intermediate`/`sum`, both heap seed decoders and their internals, and two `Copy`-source defects in `keygen.rs`. **268 tests at the time, three green runs, all six gates PASS. `make check-zeroize-bounds` is the falsifier — ~~now FIVE parts~~ five parts AT B-22; it is SIX as of B-23** (**274 tests as of B-24**), the fifth still pinning **thirteen named sites** — ⚠ **one was RETIRED by B-24, not lost: `Zeroizing(entropy)`'s `Copy`-source guard is gone because the producer now hands out a wiping type, so there is no bare source to guard** — with three controls that each run through the real detector. ⚠ **Corrected by the commit that falsified it** — a count in a status block is a claim about the CURRENT tree, and B-23 is the next commit after this sentence was written. `REVIEW-029` (the decision) and `REVIEW-030` (round two, the fixes, **two external legs** — which is what B-21's round two lacked).

**Five things B-22 established which a session will otherwise get wrong:**

- ⚠⚠ **WRAPPING A `Copy` TYPE IN A ZEROIZING WRAPPER DOES NOT WIPE THE SOURCE, AND THIS SESSION HIT IT FOUR TIMES.** `Zeroizing(entropy)` on a `[u8; 16]`, `Zeroizing(*sk.as_bytes())` on a `[u8; 32]`, and `Zeroizing::new(sha512half(&m))` — **the last of these was written INTO THE COMMIT THAT FIXED THE FIRST**, four hundred lines away, and found by both round-two legs (E-178, E-181). ⚠ **A wrapper around a `Copy` value copies; the original binding stays live.** The fix is either to bind and wipe the source, or — better — to build the value *into* the wiping buffer so no bare temporary ever exists.
- ⚠⚠ **THE RULING SAID THREE SCALARS WERE IN SCOPE, THE BUILD WIPED NONE OF THEM, AND A COMMENT CALLED THAT "THE CRATE'S BOUNDARY, NOT AN OMISSION".** Both round-two legs found it independently; a compile probe then showed `k256::NonZeroScalar` **and** `k256::Scalar` both implement `Zeroize`, so nothing had prevented it (E-181). ⚠ **This is precisely what `CLAUDE.md`'s two-round rule predicts — the construction was sound and the DESCRIPTION was hiding a real gap.** A session that reads its own fix report instead of the ruling will ship this.
- ⚠⚠ **A `Zeroizing` WRAPPED AROUND AN EXISTING BINDING HAS NO COMPILE-TIME FALSIFIER, AND THAT IS MEASURED (E-179).** Reverting `sha512half_zeroizing`'s **return type** breaks the build; reverting `Zeroizing::new(base58check_decode(..))` to the bare call gives **zero errors**, because `Zeroizing<T>` derefs to `T` and every use site compiles identically. ⚠ **Applying the revert machinery to those sites would have shipped a false pass of E-164's shape.** A source check is the honest instrument, and its guarantee is over a **NAMED SET** — a gate cannot prove no unlisted site exists.

- **`tesSUCCESS` was not accepted as the evidence, and that is the standard now.** All four of XLS-0096 §10.5's state changes were checked against ledger state before and after — public balance, `ConfidentialOutstandingAmount`, version, and the **decrypted** remainder. A `tesSUCCESS` alone does not distinguish a correct homomorphic subtraction from a lucky one.

**Status 2026-08-20 — architecture §6 step 6 is BUILT AND EXECUTED.** Real key generation and onboarding. **Issue #11 is discharged**: `lsfDisableMaster`, a regular key and a signer list each — on their own — flip the recommended key source to `standalone` and make the ruling's condition-2 warning mandatory, and the disclosures reach the holder **before the seed is asked for**. ⚠ **Issue #10 is NOT discharged and no code discharges it**: the derivation is specified in one repository document and is not a published standard, so a holder who has their seed and not this repository cannot reconstruct their key — which is the entire benefit the ruling trades a permanent decryption credential for. **Publishing an XLS informational draft is a Desktop-project decision, not a coding-session one.**

**Three things step 6 established that a session will otherwise get wrong:**

- **The ElGamal key now has TWO named sources**, and a profile declares which. `derived-from-master-seed` is the ruled construction and carries **no ElGamal secret in the profile at all**; `standalone` is the library's CSPRNG in `elgamal_sk`/`elgamal_pk` — which is what every profile before this milestone silently was. An absent `elgamal_key_source` reads as `standalone` and is **not** upgraded.
- **A registered key is not "unrecoverable", and saying so is a defect.** The protocol has no rotation and no recovery (P-10) — that is about **XLS-96**. A *derived* key is reconstructible from the master seed under the W-CONF derivation, which is the only thing deriving buys, and the confirmation said the opposite for one commit (E-125). ⚠ These are two sentences about two layers and merging them is how the banner also came to claim XLS-0096 governs XRPL account keys (E-126).
- **`from_parts` accepted a public key that was not `sk·G`.** Now `try_from_parts`, which recomputes it. The failure it allowed is the worst one this protocol offers: register a key nobody holds the secret for, encrypt every balance to it, and have every step succeed (E-120).

**ADR-0001 is `ACCEPTED` as of 2026-08-18** (`REVIEW-013c`). The last item — re-weigh Option 2 (browser WASM) on risk alone — was run: two independent legs, **both ruling Option 3**, both handed the strongest arguments against it. **Option 3 is confirmed on risk alone**, which is what rev 3 asked for and what the ADR previously could not do.

**Three things that rotation established, which a session will otherwise get wrong:**

- **The build-cost table was INVERTED, not merely stale.** Option 2 (browser WASM) is now the **cheapest** option — three published npm packages, no patching, no vendoring, no build step (E-53) — and Option 3 is the **most expensive**: a vendored C fork, an FFI binding, a Rust binary, OS-mediated IPC, a separate confirmation UI. **Option 3 was chosen anyway, on risk.** Do not repeat "Option 2 is expensive"; it is not.
- **An argument this project made three times was FALSE.** "Before the keygen ruling, an Option 2 page compromise did not touch spending authority" — false; the ADR's own table says Option 2's page can spend. The correct statement is that the keygen ruling **removes Option 2's escape hatch** (the browser can no longer delegate signing and hold only an ElGamal key, because the derivation input is the master seed) and **welds a rotatable exposure to an unrotatable one**. Use that form.
- ~~**`Accepted` unblocks architecture §6 step 7 and nothing else.** Steps 4 and 6 have their own gates, still shut.~~ **Both gates are now open.** Step 4 was built 2026-08-18 against A4–A9; step 6 was built and executed 2026-08-20. ⚠ **Step 7's own gates are not** — B-15 requires loopback, corroboration or a `tapFailHard` submitter, ADR-0002 is `Proposed`, and E-117's custody cost is unpriced.

**Rulings closed 2026-08-20** (see `docs/reviews/`): **B-14** — the transaction's ECDSA nonce is **hedged**, because the issue #1 ruling extends to it (`REVIEW-018`, E-109); ~~⚠ **secp256k1 only, ed25519 is B-16 and is the live path.**~~ **B-16 IS RULED TOO — 2026-08-27, `REVIEW-024`, E-158 — and NOT BUILT** (see the 2026-08-27 status block above). **B-15** — one ledger endpoint stands for this artifact **as a named risk acceptance** with a mandatory disclosure, and is a **gate on step 7** (`REVIEW-019`, E-110). **ADR-0002 round two** produced **revision 3**, which splits a Decision that asserted what the ADR reopened two sections later (`REVIEW-017c`, E-111) — **Decision A, native XLS-66 rejected, is settled and is what building proceeds on; Decision B, an XLS-65 `Vault` on the funding side, is open and gates the funding side only.**

⚠ **ADR-0002 is STILL `Proposed` — but on item 4 alone, which is research and not a decision.** ~~Its item 2 is a scope question that the ADR reserves for whoever owns scope~~ — **discharged 2026-08-20 in rev 4 (E-115), and NOT on the scope question.** Blocker 1 makes the hybrid a hard fork: `Vault` share tokens cannot be confidential, so it forces **native share accounting XOR confidential investor positions**, and the accounting is commodity while the confidentiality is the whole premise. ⚠ **The funder count therefore stops mattering** — one funder or twenty, all are confidential MPT holders and the architecture does not fork. ⚠ **Reversal condition:** if `lsfMPTCanHoldConfidentialBalance` ever becomes settable on a `Vault` share issuance, re-argue it. A leg argued the question dissolved on *structural* grounds instead; that was checked and rejected (E-112).

**Not blockers of ADR-0001, but still open:**

- **The Bulletproof half of the randomness story** is issue #8, where the blocking question is not which construction but whether determinism is acceptable at all when the scalars provide the zero-knowledge property. Tracked separately; REVIEW-010c named keygen as the *last packet*, and it has landed.
- **The backlog is now ONE ruling, not three.** Sigma nonces: implemented and executed. **`r`/`ρ`: implemented 2026-08-18** in `signer/src/randomness.rs`, reproducing all nine published vectors from a second implementation written from the prose (E-75), with the A4–A9 ledger in `signer/src/store.rs` (E-77). ~~**Keygen (REVIEW-012c) is still ruled and not implemented.**~~ **BUILT AND EXECUTED 2026-08-20** — `signer/src/keygen.rs` and `signer/src/onboarding.rs`, reproducing both published vectors from an implementation written against the ruling's prose, with a Devnet account holding a confidential position under a derived key (E-118). **The randomness backlog is now empty except for issue #8.** ~~⚠ **`tools/` still calls `mpt_generate_blinding_factor`** — the harnesses were not migrated, and `r`/`ρ` is implemented *in the signer*, not everywhere (E-76).~~ **CLOSED 2026-08-24 (E-132).** Eight transaction-building harnesses derive through `tools/wconf-randomness.ts`, which reproduces the same nine published vectors **before it will derive anything**, and a Send built the migrated way was accepted on Devnet. ⚠ **FIVE call sites reach upstream's generator deliberately**, each with its reason at its own call site, and **`tools/check-blinding-sources.ts` fails if that list is ever wrong**. ⚠ **The count has been wrong twice in two days, in both directions** — **four** from a name-based sweep that missed a harness which submits to Devnet (E-137), then **nine** from counting files the gate flagged rather than call sites, two of which were the gate itself and a dead entry its own stale check was hardcoded to skip (E-141). **A sweep recorded in prose is a claim with no falsifier — and a gate that reports a number is making a claim about what the number counts.**
- **The `r`/`ρ` store amendments A1–A3 were reviewed 2026-08-18 and BOTH LEGS RULED THE SIGNER MAY NOT BE BUILT AGAINST THEM.** Six defects. They are corrected by **A4–A9**, in the same document (`REVIEW-010-RULING-r-and-rho-2026-08-18.md`) — build against those. A4–A9 are adjudicated and **not themselves reviewed**, and that is a deliberate stop under this file's own two-round rule: the next artifact is the implementation and a test that fails if it is not followed, not a third packet.

**The randomness packet, for the record, is HALF ruled.** `r` and `ρ` were ruled 2026-08-18 (REVIEW-010, adjudicated in REVIEW-010c): structured fresh CSPRNG entropy, with `sk_A` and every long-lived secret forbidden from the preimage. **Ruled, implemented in the signer 2026-08-18, and implemented everywhere 2026-08-24** — ~~but `mpt_generate_blinding_factor` is still what the `tools/` harnesses call.~~ **The Bulletproof half is open** and is issue #8, where the blocking question is not which construction but whether determinism is acceptable at all when the scalars provide the zero-knowledge property. Do not treat these as one item.

**The architecture document** (`docs/architecture/ARCHITECTURE-2026-08-18.md`, **revision 6**) is explicitly provisional: it records what the rulings so far oblige and marks what is still open. ~~It does **not** license building application logic — that still waits on ADR-0001 reaching `Accepted`.~~ **ADR-0001 is now `Accepted`, so §6 step 7 is open.** §5 of that document is the authority on which gates remain shut — ~~`r`/`ρ` (A4–A9)~~ **built**, ~~onboarding that branches on ledger state (#11)~~ **built and executed 2026-08-20**, and **publication of the keygen derivation (#10), which is open and which no code discharges.**

**Status 2026-08-19 — §6 step 2 is built and executed.** The signer reads its own sequence number, confidential balance, `ConfidentialBalanceVersion`, registration state, the issuer and auditor keys and the destination's `HolderEncryptionKey` from a node, at one pinned validated index, and **re-reads before signing**. Nine fields left the holder profile, which now carries secrets and policy only and **refuses any of the nine by name**. Executed on Devnet (E-101).

**Two things that milestone established which a session will otherwise get wrong:**

- **A wrong ledger read is a CONFIDENTIALITY break, not a rejected transaction.** `tecBAD_PROOF` is a `tec`, and a `tec` is *applied to the ledger* — so a substituted destination key makes the signer publish the amount encrypted under the substituter's key, permanently. The signer does not submit, so it cannot set the `tapFailHard` that would prevent it. `CLAIMS.md` **F-23**, read at source, **not executed**. This is why TLS is mandatory for non-loopback endpoints and why B-15 exists.
- **`amount_search_to` now bounds the BALANCE as well as the confirmation.** The balance is decrypted from the ledger, so a balance above the bound is a balance the signer refuses to check an amount against. One earlier test's scenario became unreachable through `prepare` as a result and was moved rather than deleted (E-104).

**Step 2 was built before step 6 deliberately, and it was the right order.** Issue #11 requires detecting `lsfDisableMaster`, a regular key or a signer list — that *is* a ledger read. `AccountSecurity` reads all three today; **nothing branches on them yet**, and saying otherwise claims work that does not exist.

Remaining gaps are listed in `docs/task-zero/TASK-ZERO-2026-08-13.md` §0 and in the open GitHub issues.

Start with `GETTING-STARTED-CLAUDE-CODE.md`. The first three sessions are gap closure, not building.

⚠ **WHAT IS BUILT IS READ-ONLY.** ⚠⚠ ~~*"and that is the whole reason it needed no rotation"*~~ **STRUCK 2026-09-02 — the rotation ran (`REVIEW-036`) and ruled that reasoning unsound** (E-230). Read-only bought the **signing** property and not the disclosure one. The browser talks HTTP to a local Elysia process; that process reads a rippled node and sends the signer **`Request::Status` and nothing else**. **Signing stays in `wconf-signer`.** ⚠ **`Pair` and `Prepare` are the requests that carry authority, and `tools/check-web-readonly.ts` asserts that `web/api` constructs neither** — ⚠ **that scan covers `web/api`, not the whole tier**; `web/app` is covered by a separate assertion that nothing under it reaches the socket at all. Two gate defects were found and fixed: **a falsifier condition named in architecture §6 step 8 (*"the API binds to anything but loopback"*) had NO falsifier** (E-227), and **two socket detectors disagreed with the narrower wired to the whole-tier count** — the pre-fix gate **measured** exiting 0 with a real second UDS client (E-226).

**The holder signer is a separate Rust binary, not part of the web tree.** ADR-0001 puts proof generation and transaction signing in a daemon on the holder's machine; a browser page cannot invoke a local binary, so the two live side by side. Do not try to fold the signer into the TanStack/Elysia application.

⚠ **CORRECTED 2026-08-26. This said the two *"talk over `127.0.0.1` with an origin allowlist and a session token"*, and that is the design REVIEW-003b KILLED.** Architecture §3 rule 3: *"Persist no bearer secret in the browser. ADR-0001 rev 2's pasted-token design is **withdrawn**."* An origin allowlist constrains **pages**, not **processes**, any local process can forge an `Origin` header, and the issue #1 ruling puts a hostile same-host process in scope — so a value-shaped interface plus a leaked token is a **spend oracle**.

**What the signer actually speaks is a Unix domain socket** (`signer/src/ipc.rs`), chosen because architecture §3 item 4 prefers OS-mediated IPC. Grants are scoped, short-lived and **bound to the connection**; closing the connection revokes them.

⚠ **The consequence for the web tier, and it is the first thing architecture §6 step 8 has to answer: a browser page CANNOT REACH THE SIGNER AT ALL.** `ipc.rs`: *"A browser page cannot connect at all. No web API opens a Unix socket."* That is the point — it closes the XSS-to-spend-oracle path by construction rather than by a header check. **Any step-8 design that gets a browser signing confidential transactions is a trust-boundary change and needs a full adversarial rotation before implementation, not after.**

## Keys

~~Never write ElGamal keygen code before the Cryptography Reviewer has ruled on ADR-0001 §(e).~~ **Ruled 2026-08-18, implemented and executed 2026-08-20.** The construction lives in `docs/reviews/REVIEW-012-RULING-keygen-2026-08-18.md` and **only** there — do not paraphrase it into the ADR or the architecture document. `signer/src/keygen.rs` is an *implementation* of that prose and says so; where the two disagree, the ruling wins. Derivation from the XRPL master seed is upheld, with five conditions.

**Three things about that ruling that a coding session will otherwise get wrong:**

- **Its reduction is TOTAL and has no abort path**, unlike the sigma-nonce and `r`/`ρ` rulings, which both say *abort on zero, never retry*. That is correct there, where the input is fresh entropy and an abort costs one transaction. Keygen's input is a **fixed seed**, so an abort would be permanent — that holder could never participate. Do not "fix" it back.
- **Condition 2 is not cosmetic.** Onboarding must disclose that the master seed becomes a permanent decryption credential, and the signer must **warn** when the account carries `lsfDisableMaster`, a regular key or a signer list (E-69). For those holders the master seed is not spending authority, and §(e)'s argument for derivation does not hold.
- **The registration PoK must always be passed a non-NULL `context_id`.** The library accepts NULL and then emits an account-unbound, replayable proof (F-19). rippled cannot reach that path; our signer can.

~~When keygen is written, validate it against~~ **Done 2026-08-20.** mpt-crypto's own tests — `test_pok_sk`, `test_elgamal`, `test_elgamal_verify` — are C programs over **random** keys, so `signer/tests/keygen_interop.rs` drives their *properties* with a derived key. **Necessary, not sufficient:** a constant `sk_A = 1` passes all three, and **that claim is now itself a test** — `a_constant_sk_of_one_passes_every_upstream_check` runs it and asserts they pass, which is what makes the KAT load-bearing rather than decorative. The derivation's own KAT is `tools/spike-keygen-2026-08-18/t-keygen-construction.ts` and `signer/tests/keygen_kat.rs`.

## Testing

Every capability claim needs a test that fails if the claim is false.

For confidentiality specifically, **a demo of the happy path is not evidence of confidentiality.** Two harnesses are required:

- **Observer harness** — shows exactly what a full-ledger observer sees. Its first test is finding F-1 in `CLAIMS.md`: recompute the canonical `EncZero` independently and check whether freshly-initialised and post-merge balances are publicly identifiable as zero.
- **Issuer-view tool** — a single CLI command (`tools/issuer-decrypt-balance.ts`) that reads one account's `sfIssuerEncryptedBalance` and decrypts it given the issuer key. Not a standalone application. Showing what the issuer sees is the honest counterpart to showing what the public sees.

    73	            the amount nor the sender&rsquo;s remaining balance is negative. The copies are for the
    74	            sender, the receiver, the issuer and any auditor.
    75	          </p>
    76	          <p>
    77	            Why are both ends public? The ledger shows that no tokens are created inside the
    78	            confidential pool by keeping its total in plain view. The token records the total held in
    79	            confidential form, and every Convert and ConvertBack changes it by a published amount.
    80	          </p>
    81	        </div>
    82	        <Sources>E-9, E-33, F-24; TASK ZERO §3</Sources>
    83	      </Panel>

# PAGE: The overview, /

Devnet snapshot · signs nothing, holds no keys · not secure, not audited, not production-ready (P-5)

# W-CONF
What confidential MPT on the XRP Ledger hides, and what it does not. A research project, shown on one snapshot of the Devnet.
[nav] Overview | How it works | What anyone sees | What the issuer sees | Who can do what | Wallets | Custody

## What this site shows
XLS-96, Confidential Transfers, lets a token holder keep their balance encrypted on the public XRP Ledger. This site shows what that hides and what it does not, from one snapshot of the Devnet test network.
Hidden: Each holder’s balance, though some zero balances are recognisable, and the amount of each confidential send.
Public: Who sends to whom, when and how often, and every amount moved into or out of confidential form.
The issuer: Can always read every balance. No setting turns this off.
New to this? Read how it works

## Where to go
- How it works: confidential transfers in plain words, and the example this project built.
- What anyone sees: what a ledger observer reads of four test accounts, including which balances are visibly zero.
- What the issuer sees: the issuer’s encrypted copy of each balance, without the figure.
- Who can do what: what each kind of key can and cannot do.
- Wallets: why the browser wallets examined cannot hold a confidential position.
- Custody: where confidentiality and custody approval policies conflict.

## About this site
Every value comes from one snapshot of the ledger, taken when this site was built. The site signs nothing and holds no keys. No code of this project runs on a server when you load it, and your browser requests only this site’s own files.
To transact, run it yourself. Signing happens only in wconf-signer , a separate program on the holder’s own machine, never in a web page. The README’s “Run it” explains how to build it and run the local version of this site. It does not yet explain how to create a holder profile and funded Devnet accounts, which a transaction needs.

## What it never claims
- P-4 No key source hides identities. The sender and receiver of every confidential transaction are public.
- P-9 A holder is never private from the issuer. The issuer can always decrypt.
- P-10 No key source supports rotation or recovery. XLS-96 supports neither.
- P-11 No key source hides who transacts, when, or how often. Only amounts are hidden.
- F-1 A newly created confidential balance is publicly identifiable as exactly zero.
- F-24 Retiring a position in tranches publishes each tranche size.
- P-5 None of this is secure, audited, non-custodial or production-ready, and the custody mode is a simulation.
Each label is a row in the repository’s CLAIMS.md.

# PAGE: How it works, /how-it-works

Devnet snapshot · signs nothing, holds no keys · not secure, not audited, not production-ready (P-5)

# W-CONF
What confidential MPT on the XRP Ledger hides, and what it does not. A research project, shown on one snapshot of the Devnet.
[nav] Overview | How it works | What anyone sees | What the issuer sees | Who can do what | Wallets | Custody

## Confidential balances, in brief

The XRP Ledger is public: anyone can read every account and every transaction on it. Multi-Purpose Tokens (MPTs, XLS-33) are one of its kinds of token. Confidential Transfers (XLS-96) let an MPT holder keep their balance encrypted on that public ledger.
Each confidential balance is stored as an ElGamal ciphertext: a number only the right key can read. A holder registers their own encryption key when they opt in.
The ledger must still check that nobody spends more than they hold. So each confidential transaction carries zero-knowledge proofs, which every validator checks without learning the amount.
When this page was written, on 2026-10-21, XLS-96’s amendment, ConfidentialTransfer, was enabled on Devnet and not on Mainnet or Testnet.
Sources: E-1; tools/check-amendments.ts, run 2026-10-21

## The life of a confidential position

1. In: Convert [chip: amount public]
ConfidentialMPTConvert
Moves tokens from the holder’s public balance into confidential form. The amount is published. The first Convert also registers the holder’s key, which can never be changed.

2. Inside: Send [chip: amount hidden]
ConfidentialMPTSend
Moves an amount from one confidential balance to another. The amount is hidden; the sender and receiver are not. It arrives in the receiver’s inbox, and a MergeInbox moves it into their spending balance.

3. Out: ConvertBack [chip: amount public]
ConfidentialMPTConvertBack
Moves tokens back to a public balance. The amount is published, on every ConvertBack separately.

Only Send hides an amount. Its proofs show that the sender holds the key to their balance, that every encrypted copy of the amount is the same number, and that neither the amount nor the sender’s remaining balance is negative. The copies are for the sender, the receiver, the issuer and any auditor.
Why are both ends public? The ledger shows that no tokens are created inside the confidential pool by keeping its total in plain view. The token records the total held in confidential form, and every Convert and ConvertBack changes it by a published amount.
Sources: E-9, E-33, F-24; TASK ZERO §3

## What is hidden, and what is public

### Hidden from the public
- Each holder’s balance, except in the zero cases under “Public, always”.
- The amount of each Send.
Both are hidden from the public, not from the issuer.

### Public, always
- Who sends to whom, and when, so how often anyone transacts.
- Every amount converted in or out, each one separately.
- The token’s total supply, and the total held in confidential form.
- That a balance is exactly zero, in three cases: when it is first set up, when a MergeInbox empties the inbox, and after a clawback. A balance spent down to zero looks like any other.
The public numbers also bound the hidden ones. If a holder converts in 500, receives nothing and converts back 400, anyone can work out that the other 100 is either still held or has left by confidential sends. No key is needed.
Sources: P-4, P-11, F-24, F-1, E-211, R-1

## Who can read a balance, and who can spend it
- The holder can read their own balance, with their key.
- The issuer can always read every balance. The protocol keeps a second copy of each balance, encrypted to the issuer’s key, and no setting turns it off.
- An auditor can too, if the issuer names one. Only one auditor is supported.
- This was run, not inferred: the holder, the issuer and the auditor each read the same balance, and again after it changed.
- Only the holder can spend. A Send’s proof cannot be made without the holder’s key. Where that key is derived from the account’s master seed, whoever holds the seed holds the key too.
Sources: P-9, E-58, E-11, E-33

## The example: a confidential receivables facility

A bank pays a large buyer’s suppliers early, against their invoices. How much a supplier draws says a lot about its cash position, so these numbers are commercially sensitive.
This project built that facility on XLS-96 and ran it on Devnet, in 28 validated transactions:
- The bank creates the token. A Dedicated Account, an ordinary XRPL account, converts the whole float into confidential form in one Convert.
- Each supplier enrols: the bank sends it a small public payment, and the supplier runs its own Convert, which registers its key.
- Drawdowns and repayments are Sends between the Dedicated Account and the suppliers.
- The facility is retired in tranches, each one a ConvertBack.

### Anyone can see
- The size of the float.
- Which suppliers are enrolled, and both public amounts of each enrolment.
- Who drew and repaid, on which days, and how often.
- The size of every retirement tranche.

### Hidden from the public
- Each supplier’s limit.
- The size of each drawdown and repayment.
- What each supplier still owes.
The bank, as issuer, sees all of it.
In short, it hides the shape of the book, not its size.

These pages do not show the facility. They read four Devnet test accounts that hold one demo token, made by this project while it was being built: Holder A, an active position; Holder B, whose key is derived from its master seed; Holder C, the account the project’s ed25519 signing ran on; and Holder D, an early test account. The facility’s run is recorded in the repository.
The facility walkthrough
Sources: E-146, F-24, F-26, R-1

## Limits
- No key rotation or recovery. A registered key can never be changed. If a holder loses it, the balance cannot be spent, and the only remedy is an issuer clawback, which destroys the balance. A draft standard, XLS-99, proposes rotation and recovery; on 2026-10-20 Mainnet, Testnet and Devnet did not know its amendment.
- The issuer can act without the holder’s consent. If the token allows clawback, the issuer can destroy a holder’s whole confidential balance. Unless the token’s flags were made unchangeable when it was created, the issuer can also turn on locking later and freeze balances. That second power was read in rippled’s source, not run.
- Not audited. This is a research project on a test network. It is not audited, not production-ready and not safe to put value behind.
Sources: P-10, E-9, E-341, E-12, E-21, E-290, E-292, P-5
Each id under a panel, such as E-58, is a row in the project’s claims register, CLAIMS.md. Where this page and a row disagree, the row wins.

# CLAIMS register

**The register.** Every capability claim in a README, demo, post or conversation gets an entry here with the test result or primary citation that supports it. **Before publishing anything, diff the new claims against this register.**

**Human-gated checklist, not automation.** CI cannot judge whether prose overclaims. Do not add a CI job and call it solved.

## Standing prohibitions — never claim

| # | Claim | Why |
|---|---|---|
| P-1 | That this work makes XRPL quantum-safe or quantum-resistant | It does not |
| P-2 | That an application-layer PQ scheme protects funds at the ledger level | An adversary who breaks secp256k1 signs a valid classical transaction and the network accepts it |
| P-3 | That any amendment is live or enabled, without a dated `feature` RPC check | Amendment state is a reading, not knowledge |
| P-4 | That a Confidential MPT demo hides identities | It hides amounts and balances. Sender and receiver remain public |
| P-5 | That anything here is trustless, non-custodial, decentralised, audited, production-ready or secure | None of it is; ADR-0001 names the trusted parties |
| P-6 | That anything is compliant with regulation in a named jurisdiction | Not a compliance project |
| P-7 | That analysis of published work is original research | Cite Cenk, Malhotra, Akinyele, Chen, Xie, Qian by name where the work is theirs. **Add Tess Dore (2026-08-16):** the compact sigma protocol, the twisted-ElGamal analysis and the Bulletproofs++ analysis are Dore & Cenk, RippleX Research — Dore is *not* an XLS-0096 author and is easy to omit by copying E-1's list |
| P-8 | Any benchmark number without hardware, parameter set and methodology | Includes re-quoting XLS-0096 §14.2's "laptop-class CPU" timings — see B-1 |
| P-9 | That holders are private from the issuer | The issuer's decryption mirror is mandatory. No configuration makes this false |
| P-10 | That XLS-96 supports key rotation or key recovery | It supports neither, at any level |
| P-11 | That confidential transfers hide *who* transacts, or *when*, or *how often* | Only amounts are hidden. The counterparty graph and event timing are fully public |
| P-12 | **Any claim that a source does NOT say something — *nothing documents it*, *no such field*, *not exported*, *nobody has called it out*, *I could not find it* — without the search that would falsify it recorded alongside** | It is an assertion about a whole corpus and one search settles it. **Three graded rows failed this way on 2026-08-26** (E-155, E-156), two of them **positives**: U-15 quoted a sentence XLS-0096 has never contained; U-12 said a property was *"not called out anywhere I found"* when the spec states it **twice**, once in wording identical to the benefit claimed as an original reading. ⚠ **This shape survives review because it does not look like a claim** — a quotation has quotation marks, a benchmark visibly wants a methodology, and *"nobody has documented this"* reads as modesty. Gated by `tools/check-negative-claims.ts` |

| E-33 | **Generating a `ConfidentialMPTSend` proof requires the sender's ElGamal secret key `sk_A` as a witness.** `sk_A` appears in the witness `w = (m, r, b, ρ, sk_A)`; balance linkage is proved as `B₂ − b·G = sk_A·B₁` precisely because the historical randomness `r_b` is unavailable to the prover. 2-special soundness extracts `sk_A`; knowledge soundness holds in the ROM under DL. **ADR-0001's central premise is confirmed.** `ConvertBack` shares the relation; `Clawback` requires `sk_iss` instead | `cmpt-compact-sigma.pdf` §2.3, §2.4 Eq. 1, Thm 4.2 (Relations 5–6), Thm 4.4, Remark 4.5 — Dore & Cenk, RippleX Research, 2026-05-12. | E-34 | **Nonce reuse in a compact-form sigma proof leaks `sk_A`, and is undetectable from the proofs.** Compact form transmits `(e, z…)` not the commitments, so reused nonces yield proofs that verify normally while allowing an observer holding both to extract the witness. ⚠ **That mitigation line is FALSE and was falsified by two independent cryptography reviewers on 2026-08-17 (REVIEW-005a, REVIEW-005b, adjudicated in REVIEW-005c §1).** `statement` does not include `TransactionContextID` as the paper defines it, while the Fiat–Shamir challenge does — so an ordinary resubmission at a changed sequence or `CB_S_Version`, with cached ciphertexts, yields two proofs sharing first-round commitments under distinct challenges. That is Theorem 4.2's extraction condition exactly. **The formula as written causes the failure it is quoted to prevent.** The correct requirement is that the nonce preimage must refine the challenge preimage — every byte that can influence the challenge, other than the commitments, must appear injectively in the derivation. See F-17 | `cmpt-compact-sigma.pdf` §6.1, Remark 6.1. **Direct input to ADR-0001 §(e) and the Rust signer — ranks above TOB-RIPCTX-5, since it needs only a coding error, not an adversary with local measurement** | A |

# CLAIMS register

⚠ **`tapFailHard` in this document is THIS PROJECT'S SHORTHAND and appears zero times in rippled** — the real names are `fail_hard` (the RPC parameter) and `TapFailHard` (the internal apply flag). See [`docs/VOCABULARY.md`](docs/VOCABULARY.md). The code always used the real one.

**The register.** Every capability claim in a README, demo, post or conversation gets an entry here with the test result or primary citation that supports it. **Before publishing anything, diff the new claims against this register.**

**Human-gated checklist, not automation.** CI cannot judge whether prose overclaims. Do not add a CI job and call it solved.

| **Statuses** | `SUPPORTED` evidence attached · `PENDING` asserted, evidence not attached, **may not be published** · `BLOCKED` never claim · `RETRACTED` was claimed, found wrong — **keep the row** |

## Standing prohibitions — never claim

| # | Claim | Why |
|---|---|---|
| P-1 | That this work makes XRPL quantum-safe or quantum-resistant | It does not |
| P-2 | That an application-layer PQ scheme protects funds at the ledger level | An adversary who breaks secp256k1 signs a valid classical transaction and the network accepts it |
| P-3 | That any amendment is live or enabled, without a dated `feature` RPC check | Amendment state is a reading, not knowledge |
| P-4 | That a Confidential MPT demo hides identities | It hides amounts and balances. Sender and receiver remain public |
| P-5 | That anything here is trustless, non-custodial, decentralised, audited, production-ready or secure | None of it is; ADR-0001 names the trusted parties |
| P-6 | That anything is compliant with regulation in a named jurisdiction | Not a compliance project |
| P-7 | That analysis of published work is original research | Cite Cenk, Malhotra, Akinyele, Chen, Xie, Qian by name where the work is theirs. **Add Tess Dore (2026-08-16):** the compact sigma protocol, the twisted-ElGamal analysis and the Bulletproofs++ analysis are Dore & Cenk, RippleX Research — Dore is *not* an XLS-0096 author and is easy to omit by copying E-1's list |
| P-8 | Any benchmark number without hardware, parameter set and methodology | Includes re-quoting XLS-0096 §14.2's "laptop-class CPU" timings — see B-1 |
| P-9 | That holders are private from the issuer | The issuer's decryption mirror is mandatory. No configuration makes this false |
| P-10 | That XLS-96 supports key rotation or key recovery | It supports neither, at any level |
| P-11 | That confidential transfers hide *who* transacts, or *when*, or *how often* | Only amounts are hidden. The counterparty graph and event timing are fully public |
| P-12 | **Any claim that a source does NOT say something — *nothing documents it*, *no such field*, *not exported*, *nobody has called it out*, *I could not find it* — without the search that would falsify it recorded alongside** | It is an assertion about a whole corpus and one search settles it. **Three graded rows failed this way on 2026-08-26** (E-155, E-156), two of them **positives**: U-15 quoted a sentence XLS-0096 has never contained; U-12 said a property was *"not called out anywhere I found"* when the spec states it **twice**, once in wording identical to the benefit claimed as an original reading. ⚠ **This shape survives review because it does not look like a claim** — a quotation has quotation marks, a benchmark visibly wants a methodology, and *"nobody has documented this"* reads as modesty. Gated by `tools/check-negative-claims.ts` |

| E-4 | Total Send payload is **1210 B without an auditor and 1276 B with one — both now MEASURED.** The conflicting 1177 B is **wrong for the wire** | **RESOLVED 2026-08-17 by measurement.** Three `ConfidentialMPTSend` transactions serialised and accepted on standard Devnet. Each encrypted-amount field carries a **full 66-byte ElGamal pair**, not a bare 33-byte `C₂`: `SenderEncryptedAmount` 66, `DestinationEncryptedAmount` 66, `IssuerEncryptedAmount` 66, `AmountCommitment` 33, `BalanceCommitment` 33, `ZKProof` 946 = **1210 B**. The whole signed blob is **1423 B**. **Both documents were partly right and the reason matters (→ F-13):** `C₁` *is* shared, and this is **enforced by the protocol, not chosen by our harness** — a distinction REVIEW-004b HIGH-03 was right to demand and which the original evidence could not support, since it amounted to the harness observing its own input. Settled by negative control (REVIEW-004c §3): a Send built with independent per-participant randomness is refused at three layers — `mpt_get_confidential_send_proof` returns `-1` and generates nothing, `mpt_verify_send_proof` returns FAIL, and **rippled returns `tecBAD_PROOF`** where the shared-`C₁` control returns `tesSUCCESS`. The ledger nonetheless transmits `C₁` **once per participant**. The paper's 1177 is the size this would be if `C₁` were sent once, which rippled 3.3.0 does not do. The 99 B is exactly the 3 redundant 33-byte `C₁` copies at n=4. Our arithmetic was right; the paper's assumption about the wire was not. **The auditor case was measured on 2026-08-17**, closing the n=3 limitation the claims-check gate had flagged: an issuance carrying `sfAuditorEncryptionKey` was built and a four-participant Send accepted. Payload **exactly 1276 B** — `SenderEncryptedAmount` 66, `DestinationEncryptedAmount` 66, `IssuerEncryptedAmount` 66, **`AuditorEncryptedAmount` 66**, `AmountCommitment` 33, `BalanceCommitment` 33, `ZKProof` 946. Signed blob **1492 B** (n=3: 1423). The arithmetic prediction was confirmed rather than merely assumed, and **the paper's 1177 for n=4 is now refuted against a direct n=4 measurement rather than against a hypothetical** | **A on both figures, measured** |

74:| E-33 | **Generating a `ConfidentialMPTSend` proof requires the sender's ElGamal secret key `sk_A` as a witness.** `sk_A` appears in the witness `w = (m, r, b, ρ, sk_A)`; balance linkage is proved as `B₂ − b·G = sk_A·B₁` precisely because the historical randomness `r_b` is unavailable to the prover. 2-special soundness extracts `sk_A`; knowledge soundness holds in the ROM under DL. **ADR-0001's central premise is confirmed.** `ConvertBack` shares the relation; `Clawback` requires `sk_iss` instead | `cmpt-compact-sigma.pdf` §2.3, §2.4 Eq. 1, Thm 4.2 (Relations 5–6), Thm 4.4, Remark 4.5 — Dore & Cenk, RippleX Research, 2026-05-12. 108:| E-58 | **The auditor view is executed, not inferred.** With an issuance carrying `sfAuditorEncryptionKey`, the auditor's ElGamal key decrypts a holder's `sfAuditorEncryptedBalance` to the exact plaintext balance, matching what the holder reads with their own key and what the issuer reads from the issuer mirror. Read 500 immediately after the Convert, then **re-derived independently as 475 after a 25-unit Send** — the three views track each other through a balance change, which is the stronger statement | Executed 2026-08-17 on issuance `00453A7DD67EB7E60002C33AAD59E7F544C136A8D30F5D52`. **Three parties decrypt the same balance: holder, issuer, auditor — verified twice, at two different balances.** Reinforces P-9 and P-4 — this is a confidentiality model with mandatory issuer visibility and optional third-party visibility, and neither is hideable from the holder's side | A |
25:| P-4 | That a Confidential MPT demo hides identities | It hides amounts and balances. Sender and receiver remain public |
26:| P-5 | That anything here is trustless, non-custodial, decentralised, audited, production-ready or secure | None of it is; ADR-0001 names the trusted parties |
30:| P-9 | That holders are private from the issuer | The issuer's decryption mirror is mandatory. No configuration makes this false |
31:| P-10 | That XLS-96 supports key rotation or key recovery | It supports neither, at any level |
32:| P-11 | That confidential transfers hide *who* transacts, or *when*, or *how often* | Only amounts are hidden. The counterparty graph and event timing are fully public |
built 2026-09-09. `make break-emphasis-gate` is the mutations that verify it and
`make break-emphasis-gate-self-test` verifies those.

⚠⚠ **Three adversarial rounds ran on this gate — `REVIEW-043`, `-044`, `-045` —
and the rotation is CLOSED at three, which DEPARTS from the two-round rule's
own extension clause.** That clause owes a further round whenever the last one's
stopping condition did not fire, and round three's did not. **The rule is not
amended; this artifact is an exception with a stated reason**: all three rounds

# What "confidential" actually means here

- **Date:** 2026-09-02
- **Audience:** anyone deciding whether XLS-96 does what they need
- **Devnet only.** No mainnet writes, at any phase, for any reason.

This document answers one question, in plain English: **if the amount is
published every time value enters and leaves confidential form, what is
confidential about a confidential position?**

It is a fair challenge, and the honest answer is that the name promises more
than the protocol delivers. Nothing here is a complaint about the design — the
boundary is public for a good reason, given below.

---

## The short answer

**Your balance while you hold it, and the amount of each transfer between
holders. Nothing else.**

Confidential **while it circulates** — not confidential end to end.

---

## The analogy

Picture a **shared vault with a public scale at the door.**

| what happens | who can see it |
|---|---|
| You carry money **in** and it is weighed at the door | ⚠ **Everyone.** The weight is called out and written down |
| You carry money **out**, weighed again | ⚠ **Everyone**, and **each trip separately** — not just your total for the day |
| A public display shows the **total** currently inside the vault | ⚠ **Everyone** |
| Inside, your money sits in an **opaque bag** | Hidden. Nobody can see how much is in your bag |
| You hand some to another bag-holder, inside the vault | Hidden. The **amount** is not visible |
| **Who** walked up to the vault, **when**, and **how often** | ⚠ **Everyone.** Cameras at the door, always on |
| The **vault operator** holds a master key to every bag | ⚠ **Reads everything, always. No setting turns this off** |
| A bag that has **never been used** | ⚠ **Visibly empty.** It has a distinctive look nobody can fake |
| A bag you have **spent down** to empty | Looks like any other bag |

**What is hidden is the distribution inside the vault. What is public is the
perimeter, the total, and the traffic.**

---

## The same thing in the real system

| the analogy | the protocol |
|---|---|
| weighed at the door, going in | `ConfidentialMPTConvert` — publishes `MPTAmount` in plaintext |
| weighed at the door, going out | `ConfidentialMPTConvertBack` — publishes `MPTAmount`, **on every individual transaction** |
| public display of the total inside | `sfConfidentialOutstandingAmount`, a plaintext field on the issuance |
| the opaque bag | your confidential balance, an ElGamal ciphertext |
| handing money to another bag-holder | `ConfidentialMPTSend` — **the only operation that hides an amount** |
| cameras at the door | sender, receiver and timestamp of every transaction, public forever |
| the vault operator's master key | the issuer's mandatory decryption mirror (`CLAIMS.md` **P-9**) |
| the visibly empty bag | the canonical encrypted zero (**F-1**) |

---

## Why the door has to be public

This is not an oversight, and it is worth understanding before judging the design.

A public ledger has to prove that **nobody minted value inside the vault**. It
does that by keeping the running total in the clear and checking that every
crossing changes that total by exactly the declared amount. **Hiding the
crossings too would mean proving supply conservation without being able to read
any of the numbers** — far heavier machinery than this protocol uses.

`Convert` and `ConvertBack` are the mint-and-burn boundary. **Boundaries are
where the accounting has to be legible.**

---

## What it actually buys you

Take the receivables facility this repository builds.

A bank converts a float into confidential form, then draws down to suppliers
**A**, **B** and **C**. Later they repay, and the facility retires in tranches.

**An outside observer learns:**

- the size of the float, exactly
- that A, B and C each deal with the bank, and on which days
- how often each of them transacts
- the size of every retirement tranche
- the total outstanding at any moment

**They do not learn:**

- A's credit limit
- what B drew down last Tuesday
- what C still owes

⚠ **And crucially, A cannot see B's terms.** In receivables finance the
commercially sensitive facts are per-counterparty pricing and exposure, and
those are genuinely hidden. **That is the real product.**

---

## The three limits, stated plainly

**1. The public perimeter constrains the hidden interior — by arithmetic, not by
decryption.**

If a holder converts in 500, receives nothing, and converts back 400, ~~then 100
left by transfer~~ the other 100 is either still held or has left by confidential
transfer (corrected 2026-10-21, `CLAIMS.md` R-7). Anyone can do that subtraction. No key required. The public
edges and totals **bound** the hidden values, and in a small enough system they
pin them exactly.

**2. The exit is granular, not aggregate.**

⚠ **This project got this wrong in its own walkthrough and had to correct it.**
Retiring in tranches publishes **every tranche size**, because the amount is a
plaintext field on each individual `ConvertBack` — not a single netted figure at
the end. Two tranches on our own Devnet ledger read **95** and **191**, legible
to anyone (`CLAIMS.md` **F-24**).

**3. The issuer reads everything, always.**

The decryption mirror is mandatory and no configuration removes it. ⚠ **So this
is confidentiality from the public, never from the counterparty with the most
reason to look** (**P-9**).

---

## The sentence to use

> **It hides the shape of the book, not the size of the book.**

That is real, and it is a good deal less than "confidential positions" sounds
like — which is why [`README.md`](../../README.md) states what is **public** as
plainly as what is hidden.

⚠ **If you need the amounts entering and leaving to be private too, this
protocol does not do that**, and no configuration of it will.
# A confidential receivables facility on the XRPL — how it actually works

**Date:** 2026-08-20, **revised twice on 2026-08-25 and once on 2026-08-28**
(§5's zero-balance nuance for `CLAIMS.md` **E-211**, §6's build table for the
web tier, and the amendment reading re-dated) — §3 step 4 and §4's table
for `CLAIMS.md` **F-26** (a second false disclosure sentence in this document),
§3 step 9 and §4's table for **F-24**, and §6's build table after architecture
§6 step 7 was **built and executed**. **Devnet only.** Written as the reference
an app, an explainer or a post would be built *from* — not as any of those.

⚠ **The facility now runs, and the row in §6 carries a qualification that must
travel with it**: the run was **not** under `CLAIMS.md` B-15's step-7
conditions, because the ledger source was remote under an amended ruling
(E-151). It is evidence that the transactions are well-formed and that rippled
accepts them. It is **not** evidence about the loopback obligation.

> ## ⚠ Read this box before reusing anything below
>
> **This has not been through the project's publishing protocol.** That protocol
> is deliberately not part of a coding session, and nothing here is cleared for
> external use. Every capability sentence below is written against
> `CLAIMS.md`'s standing prohibitions, and the register is the authority if the
> two ever disagree.
>
> **The one sentence that must survive any rewrite:** this design hides
> **amounts**. It does not hide **who** transacts, **with whom**, **when**, or
> **how often**, and the issuer can decrypt every balance by construction. An
> explainer that leaves that out is not a simplification of this document; it is
> a different and false claim.

---

## 1. The commercial problem, in one paragraph

A large buyer's suppliers want to be paid early; a bank will advance against the
buyer's payables. That is receivables financing, and the numbers in it are
commercially sensitive in a specific way: **a supplier's drawdown level tells you
their cash position.** Put that on a public ledger in plaintext and you have
published every supplier's working-capital stress to their competitors and to
the buyer's other counterparties. Put it on a private ledger and you have given
up most of what a shared ledger was for.

**XLS-0096 Confidential MPTs are an attempt at the middle**: amounts encrypted
on a public chain, with a decryption path reserved for the parties who are
accountable for the book.

## 2. The shape

Three roles, **one issuance**, and every participant holds a confidential
balance in it.

```
      ┌────────────────────────┐
      │  Funding bank          │  issuer of the MPT
      │  · IssuerEncryptionKey │  ── can decrypt EVERY balance, always
      │  · AuditorEncryptionKey│  ── optional second party, same power
      └───────────┬────────────┘
                  │ funds publicly, once
                  ▼
      ┌────────────────────────┐
      │  Dedicated Account     │  an ORDINARY XRPL account
      │  holds the float,      │  (not an XLS-65 Vault — see §7)
      │  confidentially        │
      └───────────┬────────────┘
                  │  ConfidentialMPTSend — amounts hidden
        ┌─────────┼─────────┬─────────┐
        ▼         ▼         ▼         ▼
     supplier  supplier  supplier   ...        each with its own
        A         B         C                  HolderEncryptionKey
```

⚠ **"Dedicated Account", never "vault".** An XLS-65 `Vault` is a different
ledger object, it *cannot* convert to a confidential balance, and the word has
already nearly derailed one reading of the design.

## 3. The walkthrough

A worked example: a bank runs a **£50m** facility for **30 suppliers** of one
large buyer.

### Setup — public, and deliberately so

**Step 1 — the bank creates the issuance.** A Multi-Purpose Token flagged to
hold confidential balances. It sets:

- **`IssuerEncryptionKey`** — mandatory. The bank can decrypt every holder's
  balance. **No configuration removes this**, and any design that assumes
  otherwise is wrong about the protocol.
- **`AuditorEncryptionKey`** — optional. A trustee or supervisor with the same
  visibility.
- **`sfDomainID`** — gates the issuance to a permissioned domain, so only
  credentialled accounts can hold it.

⚠ **`TransferFee` must be zero on a confidential issuance.** Fees and interest
settle off-ledger or as separate confidential transfers. That is a protocol
constraint, not a design choice, and it shapes everything downstream.

**Step 2 — the bank creates a Dedicated Account.** An ordinary XRPL account.
It cannot be the issuer account: **an issuer cannot convert its own issuance
into a confidential balance.** The ledger refuses it outright — this is the
reason the design needs a separate account to hold the float, not a stylistic
preference.

**Step 3 — the bank funds it publicly** with the whole £50m float, as plaintext
MPT.

### The one plaintext moment

**Step 4 — one `ConfidentialMPTConvert`.** This does two things at once: it
registers the Dedicated Account's `HolderEncryptionKey`, and it moves the entire
float into confidentiality.

**The amount is public at this step, and that is the intent.** Facility size is
what the market and the funders are entitled to see.

⚠ **~~After this, no plaintext amount appears again until the facility is
retired or resized.~~ That sentence was FALSE and is struck (2026-08-25,
`CLAIMS.md` F-26).** Step 5 publishes two plaintext amounts **per supplier** —
the bank's `Payment` of the enrolment token, and the supplier's own
`ConfidentialMPTConvert`, whose `MPTAmount` is a plaintext field exactly as step
4's and step 9's are. On a thirty-supplier facility that is sixty plaintext
amounts between the float conversion and the first drawdown.

**What is true, and it is what the design actually buys:** no **drawdown** and
no **repayment** publishes an amount, and those are the numbers that carry the
commercial signal. The plaintext amounts are the enrolment tokens, which are
deliberately nominal and identical, and the facility-level ones — its size, and
each tranche of its retirement.

⚠ This is the **second** false disclosure sentence found in this document
(F-24 was the first), and like F-24 it survived the document's own
`claims-check`. Both were about *which* amounts are plaintext. A sentence of the
form *"no plaintext amount appears after X"* should be assumed wrong until every
transaction type between X and the end has been listed.

### Enrolling a supplier

**Step 5.** The bank pays the supplier a token amount of the MPT publicly, and
the supplier runs its own `ConfidentialMPTConvert` — which is what registers
their `HolderEncryptionKey`.

⚠ **Registration happens exactly once and cannot be repeated.** The protocol
requires the key when initialising and forbids it afterwards. A supplier with no
registered key **cannot receive a confidential amount at all** — there is no key
to encrypt to, so the transaction cannot be built, let alone rejected.

### Running the facility

**Step 6 — drawdown.** Dedicated Account → supplier, one `ConfidentialMPTSend`.
The amount is hidden. Received value lands in the supplier's **inbox**; a
`ConfidentialMPTMergeInbox` moves it into their spendable balance.

**Step 7 — repayment.** Supplier → Dedicated Account, the same transaction type,
amount hidden.

**Step 8 — several funders?** They are confidential holders in the same
issuance. The bank sends each their position confidentially, and yield as
further confidential transfers. **No shares and no share price** — positions are
denominated directly, which is a large part of why a `Vault` buys nothing here
(§7).

### Wind-down

**Step 9 — `ConfidentialMPTConvertBack`** when the facility retires or resizes.

⚠ **Public: each ConvertBack's OWN amount, in the clear — not merely the
aggregate change.** ~~Public: the aggregate change.~~ **Corrected 2026-08-25
(`CLAIMS.md` F-24), and the earlier sentence would have misled a reader in a way
that matters:** `MPTAmount` is a plaintext field on every individual
`ConfidentialMPTConvertBack` (XLS-0096 §10.3), so retiring a facility in tranches
publishes **every tranche size**, not just the net movement in
`sfConfidentialOutstandingAmount`. Two ConvertBacks executed on 2026-08-24 read
95 and 191 straight off their validated transactions.

This is symmetric with step 4: **`Convert` and `ConvertBack` are the two
transaction types in this design that publish an amount, and both publish it per
transaction.** It is the specification's own intent — §10.7's worked example
turns on it — and not a defect.

---

## 4. Who sees what

| | Facility size | Who is enrolled | Who drew, when, how often | **Amounts** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Anyone with a block explorer | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ for drawdowns and repayments — **but every `Convert` amount, every `ConvertBack` amount and every plaintext `Payment` is public** (F-24, F-26). That is the facility's size, each retirement tranche, **and both plaintext amounts of every enrolment** |
| A supplier | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | only their own |
| **The bank (issuer)** | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | **✅ everyone's** |
| **An auditor, if configured** | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | **✅ everyone's** |

**Three tiers of disclosure, and none of them requires publishing a position:**

1. **Public** — `sfConfidentialOutstandingAmount` on the issuance keeps the
   aggregate visible, alongside the transaction graph.
2. **The arranger** — the mandatory issuer mirror.
3. **A supervisor or trustee** — the optional auditor key.

⚠ **This is a statement about who can decrypt what. It is not a compliance
claim.** Nothing here asserts that the structure satisfies any named
jurisdiction's requirements.

## 5. ⚠ What this does NOT hide

The most important section in this document, and the one most likely to be cut
from a shorter version.

**It hides the amount of a confidential *transfer*, and balances. It hides nothing else** — and ⚠ **converting in or out publishes the amount in plaintext, every time.** Only a `Send` hides one.

- **The counterparty set is public.** Every supplier on the facility is
  identifiable.
- **Timing and frequency are public.** Every drawdown and repayment is a visible
  event with a timestamp.
- **Therefore drawdown *frequency* leaks.** A supplier moving from monthly to
  weekly draws is **legible as distress without a single amount being known** —
  which is a substantial part of the commercial signal the design set out to
  protect.
- **No holder is private from the issuer.** By construction, permanently.

**The proposed mitigation for the frequency leak — scheduled cover traffic, so
the Dedicated Account sends to every supplier on a fixed cadence whether or not
value moves — is `Proposed` and has been reviewed by nobody.** It rests on
zero-amount sends being indistinguishable from real ones, which this project has
tested three ways and **has not established**. Surviving three attempts to break
a claim is not a proof of it. Do not present cover traffic as a feature.

⚠ **One thing this section did NOT say, added 2026-08-28 (`CLAIMS.md` E-211):**
**a balance can be exactly zero and not publicly identifiable as zero.** F-1's
canonical `EncZero` is used on first-time init, merge reset and clawback — so a
freshly-enrolled supplier's balance **is** publicly known to be zero, while a
supplier who has drawn and fully repaid holds a *randomised* encryption of zero
that matches nothing. **The two look completely different to an observer and
are the same number.** ⚠ The converse is the trap: **a ciphertext that does not
match the canonical zero is NOT evidence of a non-zero balance**, and the web
tier shipped a sentence saying it was.

**And two protocol constraints that shape any product built on this:**

- **Keys cannot be rotated or recovered.** A lost key is a permanently lost
  balance; a compromised key is permanently compromised.
- **Clawback, where the issuance enables it, burns the holder's *entire*
  balance.** It cannot model partial recovery. It is a sanctions instrument,
  not a repayment mechanism. (It is available only if the issuance carries
  `lsfMPTCanClawback`; without that flag the attempt is refused — a
  qualification `claims-check` caught missing here.)

the failure this project exists to avoid.

See `WEB-TIER-DEMO-SCRIPT-2026-08-28.md` |
